questions.q: Why doesn't a logical circuit diagram, by itself, tell you whether it will run efficiently on a given real device?
options: The diagram's gates assume any two qubits can interact directly, but real hardware only supports the specific pairs listed in its connectivity graph
Logical circuits only specify single-qubit gates, never two-qubit gates
Logical circuit diagrams are never used to design real quantum algorithms
Real hardware always matches whatever connectivity a logical circuit assumes
questions.explain: A logical circuit's two-qubit gates are drawn without regard to physical adjacency; a real device only supports the qubit pairs in its connectivity graph, and the mismatch is exactly what the compiler's routing step must resolve.

questions.q: What does transpilation (routing) do to a logical circuit before it runs on real hardware?
options: It simply renames the qubits without changing the gate sequence
It maps logical qubits onto specific physical qubits and rewrites any gate outside the device's connectivity graph into something the hardware can execute
It is an optional step that most circuits skip
It removes all two-qubit gates from the circuit entirely
questions.explain: Transpilation is a required translation step: it assigns physical qubits and rewrites unsupported gates (typically via SWAP insertion) so the circuit respects the device's real connectivity graph.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, two physical qubits sit at graph distance 3 apart. How many SWAPs are needed to bring them adjacent, and how many total two-qubit operations result once the logical gate is included (using 3 CNOTs per SWAP)?
options: 1 SWAP, for 4 total two-qubit operations
2 SWAPs, for 7 total two-qubit operations (6 CNOTs from SWAPs plus 1 for the logical gate)
0 SWAPs, since distance-3 qubits can interact directly
3 SWAPs, for 9 total two-qubit operations
questions.explain: Distance 3 requires distance-minus-one SWAPs (2), each costing 3 CNOTs, for 6 CNOTs, plus the 1 CNOT for the actual logical gate -- 7 total two-qubit operations where the circuit only asked for 1.

questions.q: Using a representative 0.5% error rate per two-qubit gate, roughly how does the chance of at least one error compare between the direct 1-gate version and the routed 7-operation version from the worked example?
options: The routed version has a lower error chance because SWAPs are error-free operations
About 50% for the direct gate versus about 99% for the routed version
Both versions have exactly the same error chance, since routing doesn't add real gates
About 0.5% for the direct gate versus about 3.4% for the routed version -- nearly seven times higher purely from routing
questions.explain: Using 1 − (1 − 0.005)^n, 1 operation gives about 0.5% error while 7 operations gives about 3.4% -- the routing overhead alone multiplies the error chance roughly sevenfold, even though the logical operation performed is unchanged.

questions.q: Why can a circuit that 'only needs 40 logical two-qubit gates' still blow through a device's practical error budget?
options: If the circuit's connectivity pattern mismatches the device's physical graph, routing can add significant extra gates beyond the logical count, consuming more of the limited coherence/error budget than the logical gate count suggests
Because routing overhead only affects single-qubit gates, not the overall error budget
Because 40 gates always exceeds every real device's error budget regardless of connectivity
Because logical gate count has no relationship to a circuit's real error at all
questions.explain: The real constraint is logical gate count combined with how well the circuit's connectivity matches the device -- a poor match can push a 40-gate circuit well past 60 real two-qubit operations after routing, eating into the limited depth a device can support before error dominates.
